title: Valid Anagram
description: Two strings are anagrams iff their character counts match. One Map, increment for s, decrement for t — all zero at the end means anagram. O(n).

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"Let me restate: I'm given two strings `s` and `t`, and I return `true` if `t` is an anagram of `s` — same multiset of characters, possibly rearranged. A few quick clarifying questions:"

• Are the strings case-sensitive? Is `"Listen"` an anagram of `"silent"`?
• Character set — lowercase ASCII, or full Unicode?
• Should I strip whitespace or punctuation, or treat them as significant characters?
• Is the empty-string vs empty-string case `true`? (Trivially yes — both have the empty multiset.)
sections.why: The case-sensitivity and whitespace questions are the ones that decide whether your solution actually solves the user's problem. If they say 'normalize first,' you'd add `.toLowerCase()` and possibly `.replace(/\s/g, '')` before counting. The character-set question matters less here than in Group Anagrams — you're counting, not sorting — but it still affects whether you can use a length-26 array vs. a Map.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious solutions before you discard them.
sections.say:
"Two obvious brute forces."

"One: sort both strings and compare with `===`. That's O(n log n) time, O(n) space for the sorted copies. Clean and short — a perfectly fine answer if the interviewer doesn't push for better."

"Two: count chars in `s`, then walk `t` and tick each one down — if any count goes negative or any char isn't in the count, return false. That's O(n) time, O(1) space for a bounded alphabet."

"I'll go with the count-map approach since it beats the sort asymptotically and the constant factors are similar."
sections.why: Naming the sort solution first is important — it's the obvious one, and dismissing it without acknowledging it makes you look like you skipped the easy answer to show off. By explicitly comparing the two, you show you considered both AND have a principled reason for picking the counter — not 'because it's the fancy one' but 'because it's strictly better on the asymptotic.'

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What signal in the problem points to a counter map?
sections.say:
"This is a frequency-counter hash-map problem. The structural property: two strings are anagrams iff their character frequency distributions are identical. So if I maintain a count map keyed on character, +1 walking `s` and -1 walking `t`, the strings are anagrams iff every entry settles back to zero."

"Two tricks make this even cleaner. First, length check at the top — if the lengths differ, the strings cannot be anagrams, period; bail immediately and skip the whole final zero-check. Second, while walking `t`, if any count goes negative, return false right away — that means `t` has an extra of some char that `s` didn't, and no further work can rescue it. Combined with the length check, those two short-circuits mean I never need to scan the map at the end."
sections.why: Naming the data structure AND the structural property — 'same frequency distribution → anagram' — is what the interviewer wants. The two short-circuits (length check + negative-on-decrement) aren't just micro-optimizations; they're what lets you skip the trailing zero-check entirely. Spelling out *why* they're load-bearing — not just that they're nice — is what separates pattern recognition from cargo culting.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me trace through a few cases." Three inputs — a typical anagram pair, a same-length non-anagram (where a counter goes negative), and a length-mismatch case that exits at the top.

examples.note: Classic anagram pair — counts balance to zero everywhere.
examples.trace:
length check: 7 === 7 → continue
build count from s: {a:3, n:1, g:1, r:1, m:1}
t: 'n' → count.n=0
t: 'a' → count.a=2
t: 'g' → count.g=0
t: 'a' → count.a=1
t: 'r' → count.r=0
t: 'a' → count.a=0
t: 'm' → count.m=0
walked all of t with no negatives → return true ✓

examples.note: Same length but not an anagram — the 'c' in t isn't in the count map, so we short-circuit.
Length mismatch — exits immediately at the top check, no Map even built.

sections.why: The second example is the one to mention out loud — it's the case where the negative-counter short-circuit pays off. If you didn't bail on `!count.has('c')`, you'd `set('c', -1)` and the negative check would catch it on the next line — same correctness, slightly redundant. The third example is also worth flagging because it shows the length-check top-bail is doing real work, not just being defensive.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Edges worth flagging:"

• Both empty `s=""`, `t=""` → length check passes (0 === 0), both loops are no-ops, returns `true`. Vacuously correct.
• Length mismatch → caught immediately by the top check. Don't skip this — without it, you'd need to scan the map at the end for non-zero entries.
• Repeated characters (`"aabb"`, `"abab"`) → the counter handles repeats naturally; that's what makes it stronger than a Set.
• Unicode/emoji → `for...of` on a string DOES iterate by codepoint (unlike index-based access), so this canonical actually handles emoji correctly. Worth flagging as a hidden win.
• Case sensitivity — if `"Listen"` should match `"silent"`, lowercase both at the top.
• Whitespace — same: strip if the problem says to.
sections.why: The Unicode call-out here is a positive one — `for...of` happens to do the right thing, which is the opposite of `s[i]` indexing that breaks on surrogate pairs. Naming that explicitly shows you know the difference and that this canonical wasn't an accident. The case/whitespace edges aren't trivial — they're real interview-trap territory where the candidate codes the right algorithm against the wrong specification.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(n) where n is the string length. Two passes — one over `s` to build the count map, one over `t` to decrement — each does O(1) work per character.

Space is O(1) for a bounded alphabet — the Map holds at most |alphabet| entries (26 for lowercase English, 128 for ASCII), independent of n. For unbounded Unicode it'd be O(n) in the worst case.

If you wanted to extend to 'are two strings k-anagrams' (anagrams after at most k char swaps), you'd build the count map the same way, then sum the absolute deltas and check if the total is at most 2k. Same primitive — frequency map — with a different aggregation. Or extend to 'find all anagram start indices in a longer text': that's the same counter inside a sliding window, which is exactly the Find All Anagrams in a String problem."
sections.why: The amortization is straightforward — two linear passes, O(1) per char — but the wrap-up's job is to show transfer. Naming k-anagrams AND Find All Anagrams in a String unprompted demonstrates you see this as a *template* (frequency-count comparison) that composes with sliding window, not just a one-off trick. That's the move that wins the senior-track follow-up.

reference.approach: Frequency counter (+1 over s, −1 over t)
notes: Length check first — different lengths cannot be anagrams, and it lets us skip a final zero-check.
Single Map: +1 walking s, -1 walking t. If any count goes negative, t has a char s did not have.
Space is O(1) because the alphabet is fixed; sorting both strings is O(n log n) — fine in interviews but slower.

alternates.label: Sort both strings and compare
alternates.when: Reach for this when you want the shortest possible code and O(n log n) is acceptable. Two sorted strings are anagrams iff they are identical — no Map needed. Idiomatic Python/Swift one-liner; in JS it requires spreading to avoid in-place mutation.
notes: Simpler code than the counter, but O(n log n) time vs O(n) for the counter approach.
Use [...s] (spread) not s.split('') to handle emoji / surrogate pairs correctly.
Allocates two new sorted strings — O(n) extra space even for a bounded alphabet.

reference.crux: One count map: +1 for every char in s, −1 for every char in t — equal lengths plus no count ever going negative means the multisets match, in O(n).
cruxDistractors: Sort both strings and compare them with ===; equal sorted strings are anagrams.
Put each string's characters in a Set and compare the two Sets for equality.
Add each char's code into a running sum for s and t; equal sums prove the same characters.

questions.q: Why is the length check at the top important?
options: Without it, iterating over the longer string would index past the end of the shorter one and throw
Different lengths cannot be anagrams, and skipping it would force a final scan for non-zero counts
It prevents `s` and `t` from being implicitly coerced to numbers during the loop
The Map throws when its internal load factor exceeds the size hint passed at construction
questions.explain: Equal multisets imply equal lengths, so a mismatch is an instant `false`. Without the guard a shorter `t` would leave positive leftovers the decrement loop never inspects, forcing a trailing scan of the Map for non-zero entries — nothing throws, `for...of` over `t` just stops early.

questions.q: What does it mean if a counter goes BELOW zero during the t scan?
options: t is a prefix of s, so the remaining s chars are unmatched
t contains a character that s did not — not an anagram
We've already matched every occurrence of that char and should switch to comparing the next one
It indicates a hash collision in the Map and the count for that key should be reset
questions.explain: The stored count is `s`'s remaining quota for that character, so dropping below zero means `t` spent more of it than `s` ever had. The mirror case (a count left ABOVE zero) can't happen once the lengths match.

questions.q: Why is the space complexity considered O(1) here?
options: Counts are decremented to zero, so the Map ends empty regardless of input size
The alphabet is bounded, so the Map has a fixed maximum size independent of n
The Map is allocated once at module-load time and reused across all calls
Map entries with value 0 are garbage-collected during iteration, bounding live size to O(1)
questions.explain: The Map holds one entry per DISTINCT character, capped by the alphabet (26 lowercase, 128 ASCII) rather than by n. Entries hit zero but are never deleted, so it's the fixed alphabet — not shrinkage — that bounds the size.

options: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n log n)
questions.explain: Two sequential passes — one over `s` to build the counts, one over `t` to decrement — each doing O(1) Map work per character. 2n is O(n); the sort-and-compare alternative is the O(n log n) one.

questions.q: The counter approach beats the 'sort both strings and compare' approach because:
options: Sorting allocates a new string per comparison; the counter mutates in place, avoiding GC pressure
Counting is O(n) while sorting both is O(n log n)
Sorting both strings then comparing requires O(n²) char-by-char equality checks
Sort is non-deterministic in V8 for equal-length strings, so it can return the wrong answer
questions.explain: Sorting each string costs O(n log n); the frequency-counter does it in a single linear pass, so it is asymptotically faster (sorting is still correct, just slower).

questions.q: If you increment for every char in s and decrement for every char in t, two strings are anagrams exactly when:
options: At least one count is positive, indicating s contributed something
Every count ends at zero
The sum of all counts equals the length of s
Every count in the map matches the count of the most-frequent character
questions.explain: Equal counts mean each character appeared the same number of times in both; every entry nets to zero only when the multisets match.

questions.q: Why does counting handle repeated characters correctly where a plain Set would fail?
options: A Set's `.has` returns false on the second occurrence of a value, so duplicates would be silently dropped during the s scan
A Set only records presence, losing multiplicity — `aab` vs `abb` look identical to a Set
Set iteration ordering is undefined, so comparing the s-set to the t-set requires sorting first
Set membership is checked by `==` not `===`, so `'a'` and a boxed `String('a')` would be conflated
questions.explain: Anagram validity depends on HOW MANY of each char; a Set collapses duplicates, so it cannot distinguish two a's from one, but a count map tracks the exact quantity.

questions.q: What does `isAnagram("", "")` return with this canonical?
options: false — empty strings have no characters to be anagrams of
true
undefined — neither loop runs, so the function never reaches a return statement
0 — the empty Map's size is returned implicitly
questions.explain: Lengths match (0 === 0), both loops are no-ops, and control reaches `return true` — two empty strings share the empty multiset, so they are anagrams.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the single-pass counter approach. The early-exit on negative is what keeps it O(n).

blanks.hint: strict inequality — bail when lengths differ
negative count means t has an extra character

L3.prompt: Write `isAnagram(s, t)` using one Map of character counts (O(n) time). Log `isAnagram("anagram", "nagaram")` then `isAnagram("rat", "car")`.
hints: Increment for s, decrement for t — return false the moment any count goes negative.
Equal length plus no negatives means counts balanced to zero everywhere.
